home.introduction: CSS Layout Lab is an interactive space to learn and experiment with the different ways of building layouts in CSS: from classic models like block and inline, to modern tools like flexbox and grid.
home.description: <brick>CSS Layout Lab</brick> provides <moss>clear documentation</moss> and <moss>dynamic examples</moss>, with which you can modify values and see in <moss>real time</moss> how the arrangement of <moss>elements</moss> <moss>adjusts</moss>, gaining a better understanding of the possibilities of each approach and how to apply them in your projects.

aboutMe.title: About Me
aboutMe.description:
After many years working in web development, CSS continues to amaze me with its possibilities and constant innovations. One of its most important and frequent uses is layout management, which allows you to organize and distribute the elements of a page in a flexible and precise way.

That's why I created this documentation, where I try to explain in a simple way how to create layouts with CSS and how to apply different techniques depending on the needs of each project.

This tutorial is designed for all kinds of developers, from juniors to experts. Some may discover basic concepts for the first time, while others can see in practice how certain properties behave, which are often handled by libraries like Bootstrap, exploring grid and flexbox directly.

I hope you enjoy it!

map.title: Choose where to start building
map.fundamentals: Box model, display, units and positioning: the foundations of any layout.
map.flex: Distribute elements along one axis and let them adapt to the available space.
map.grid: Control rows and columns at once to define complete structures.
map.beyond: Container queries, logical properties and recipes ready for your projects.

basicConcepts.title: Introduction to CSS Layouts
basicConcepts.description:
In CSS, a layout is the way elements are organized and distributed within a page or section. It determines where elements are placed, how they are aligned with each other, and how they adapt to the screen size.

Our goal is to show, through simple and comparative examples, how to align elements both horizontally and vertically, how to organize different sections of a page, and in which situations each technique is best applied.

We want to help you visualize, practice, and understand the essentials to improve your designs and write CSS with greater confidence and clarity.

Before diving into block, inline-block, flex, or grid, it is essential to understand some key concepts that determine how elements are positioned and behave within a web page.

boxModel.title: Box Model
boxModel.description: Every element in HTML is a box. This model defines how the space occupied by an element is calculated:
boxModel.item1: margin: The outer space, between this box and others.
boxModel.item2: border: The border surrounding the content and padding of an element, customizable in thickness, style, and color.
boxModel.item3: padding: The inner space between the content and the border.

display.title: Display
display.description: The display property determines how the box behaves. It can be:
display.item1: block: Occupies the full available width and starts on a new line.
display.item2: inline: Does not start on a new line and only takes the necessary space.
display.item3: inline-block: Like inline, but allows defining width, height, etc.
display.item4: flex and grid: Modern layout systems (we’ll see them in detail later).

axis.title: Rows and Columns
axis.description: When we talk about flex or grid, we must think in terms of rows and columns.
axis.item1: In flex, elements are arranged in a single row or column, depending on flex-direction.
axis.item2: In grid, they can be arranged in rows and columns simultaneously.
axis.item3: Understanding this structure helps control how child elements are aligned and distributed.

containers.title: Container and child
containers.description: A layout always has a hierarchy:
containers.item1: The container is the parent element that defines the context (display: flex, grid, etc).
containers.item2: The child elements behave according to the rules of that context.

gap.title: Spacing
gap.description: The gap, row-gap, and column-gap properties allow control of the spacing between elements in a flex or grid container:
gap.item1: gap: Defines uniform spacing between rows and columns.
gap.item2: row-gap: Defines only the spacing between rows.
gap.item3: column-gap: Defines only the spacing between columns.
gap.item4: These properties replace the use of margin on children, making the layout cleaner and more predictable.

responsive.title: Responsiveness
responsive.description: Nowadays, websites must be adaptable, able to adjust to different screen sizes, from mobile devices to large monitors. Modern properties like flex and grid allow creating layouts that automatically reorganize. This makes it easier to build fluid, consistent, and more maintainable designs.

units.title: Units in CSS
units.description: In CSS there are several basic units used to define measures such as sizes, margins, paddings, fonts, etc. They are divided into absolute and relative units.

absolutes.title: Absolute Units
absolutes.description: These do not change depending on context; they always measure the same.
absolutes.item1: px (pixels): Fixed unit, ideal for precise details.
absolutes.item2: cm, mm, in (centimeters, millimeters, inches): More common in print.
absolutes.item3: pt (points): Used in typography, 1pt = 1/72 of an inch.

relatives.title: Relative Units
relatives.description: These change depending on context, such as screen size or font size.
relatives.item1: % (percentage): Relative to the parent element. Very useful for fluid layouts.
relatives.item2: em: Relative to the parent’s font size. 2em = 2 times the parent’s font size.
relatives.item3: rem: Relative to the root font size (usually html). More predictable than em.
relatives.item4: vw (viewport width): 1vw = 1% of the viewport width. Useful for responsive designs.
relatives.item6: vmin: The smaller value between vw and vh.
relatives.item7: vmax: The larger value between vw and vh.
relatives.item8: svw / svh: small viewport (useful on mobile with dynamic bars).
relatives.item9: lvw / lvh: Represents the maximum possible viewport size, as if navigation bars (browser top or bottom) were hidden.
relatives.item10: dvw / dvh: Represents the current viewport size, which changes when browser bars appear or disappear.

blockInline.title: block & inline
blockInline.description: block, inline and inline-block are display models that define how HTML elements are arranged and occupy space on the page, controlling their flow, alignment, and dimensions.

block.title: block
block.item2: By default, they occupy all available width.
block.item4: They are ideal when you need elements to stack vertically and want to control size and spacing.
block.example:
In this example we have a container that contains three children with the class child set as display block, where each child occupies the full possible width of the container because they do not have a fixed width.

The class child would not need to be explicitly set as display block since by default, div elements are block (this is done for teaching purposes).

inline.title: inline
inline.description: inline elements flow in the same line as text:
inline.item1: They do not start on a new line and only occupy the necessary width.
inline.item2: They can be nested inside block or inline elements.
inline.item3: They do not allow box properties like width, height, margin-top, margin-bottom. Generally, you cannot set width or height, nor vertical margins. You can apply padding and horizontal margin.
inline.item4: They can contain only text or other inline elements.
inline.item5: They are ideal when you want content to flow inside a paragraph.
inline.example:
In this example we have a container that contains three children with the class child set as display inline, where each child only occupies the necessary width of the container. We can see how the container’s padding does not adjust to the height of its children when they are inline elements.

The class child would not need to be explicitly set as display inline since by default, span elements are inline (this is done for teaching purposes).

inlineBlock.title: inline-block
inlineBlock.description: inline-block elements combine characteristics of both inline and block elements:
inlineBlock.item1: They flow inline like inline elements but allow box dimensions like block elements.
inlineBlock.item2: They align horizontally with other inline or inline-block elements.
inlineBlock.item3: They do accept properties like width, height, padding, and margin (both vertical and horizontal).
inlineBlock.item4: They do not start on a new line but respect their own size within the inline flow.
inlineBlock.item5: They are ideal for small components like buttons, cards, or boxes that need to align horizontally but at the same time behave like a block.
inlineBlock.example: In this example we have a container that contains three children with the class child set as display inline-block, where each child occupies the width and height set in its configuration. We can see how the container adjusts to the height of its children, unlike elements set as inline.

flex.title: flex
flex.description: flex (flexbox) is a one-dimensional layout model that distributes elements in a row or column, with control over spacing and adaptive alignment (main axis) and (cross axis), achieving flexible and responsive designs. flex is ideal when you need to align elements on a single axis (horizontal or vertical) in a flexible way, adapting their size and position according to the available space.

direction.title: flex-direction
direction.description: Controls how the child elements are arranged along the main axis:
direction.item1: row (default): Places elements from left to right.
direction.item2: row-reverse: Places elements from right to left.
direction.item3: column: Places elements from top to bottom.
direction.item4: column-reverse: Places elements from bottom to top.
direction.example: With this dynamic example, we give the user the opportunity to see the different arrangements of the child elements by modifying the flex-direction property in the selector.

wrap.title: flex-wrap
wrap.description: Determines whether items should stay on a single line or wrap.
wrap.item1: nowrap (default): Everything on one line, even if it overflows.
wrap.item2: wrap: Items move to a new line if they don’t fit.
wrap.item3: wrap-reverse: Same as wrap, but wrapping occurs in reverse order.
wrap.example: With this dynamic example, we give the user the opportunity to see the different arrangements of the child elements by modifying the flex-wrap property in the selector.
wrap.tip: Combine flex-wrap: wrap with gap so the spacing also applies between wrapped lines.

justifyAlignRow.example: With this dynamic example, we give the user the opportunity to see the different arrangements of the child elements by modifying the justify-content and align-items properties in the selectors.

justify.title: justify-content <moss>(row)</moss>
justify.description: justify-content in a container with flex-direction: row, aligns the child elements horizontally inside the flex container.
justify.item4: space-between: Places the maximum possible space between elements.
justify.item5: space-around: Places equal space around the elements.
justify.item6: space-evenly: Places equal space between elements and around them.

align.title: align-items <moss>(row)</moss>
align.description: align-items in a container with flex-direction: row, aligns the child elements vertically. align-content does the same as align-items but only when there are multiple rows (flex-wrap: wrap) and they have wrapped.
align.item1: stretch (default): Stretches elements to fill the container height.
align.item2: flex-start: Aligns all elements at the top.
align.item4: flex-end: Aligns all elements at the bottom.
align.item5: baseline: Aligns elements along the text baseline.

justifyAlignRow.title: justify-content & align-items (row)

justifyAlignColumn.example: With this dynamic example, we give the user the opportunity to see the different arrangements of the child elements by modifying the justify-content and align-items properties in the selectors.

justify.title: justify-content <moss>(column)</moss>
justify.description: justify-content in a container with flex-direction: column, aligns the child elements vertically inside the flex container.
justify.item1: flex-start (default): Aligns all elements at the top of the container.
justify.item3: flex-end: Aligns all elements at the bottom of the container.
justify.item4: space-between: First element at the top, last at the bottom, others spaced in between.
justify.item6: space-evenly: Equal space between elements and around them.

align.title: align-items <moss>(column)</moss>
align.description: align-items in a container with flex-direction: column, aligns the child elements horizontally.
align.item1: stretch (default): Elements stretch horizontally to the container’s width (if no fixed width is set).
align.item2: flex-start: Aligns all elements to the left.
align.item4: flex-end: Aligns all elements to the right.

justifyAlignColumn.title: justify-content & align-items (column)

grow.title: flex-grow
grow.description: Defines how a flex item grows to fill the available extra space in the container.
grow.item2: If you set a number greater than 0, the item will grow proportionally according to that value.
grow.example: In this example, we can see how the item with the class child-1 has the default size since its flex-grow is set to 0. On the other hand, the rest of the items grow in proportion to the flex-grow value in their respective class, with the child-3 item growing twice as much as the child-2 item.

shrink.title: flex-shrink
shrink.description: Defines how a flex item shrinks when the container has less space than the sum of its items.
shrink.item2: If you set 0, that item will not shrink even if space is lacking.
shrink.example: In this example, we can see how the item with the class child-1 does not shrink because its flex-shrink is set to 0. In contrast, the other items shrink since their flex-shrink is 1.
shrink.tip: A flex item does not shrink below its content size because its min-width is auto. If long text overflows the container, add min-width: 0 to the item.

basis.title: flex-basis
basis.description: This is the base size of the item before growth or shrink is applied.
basis.item1: By default it is auto, which takes the natural size of the content or the defined width/height.
basis.item2: It can be a value in px, %, auto, rem, em, etc.
basis.example: In this example, we can see how each item takes its width according to the value assigned through the flex-basis property.
basis.tip: In a row container, flex-basis takes priority over width. In a column it acts on the height, because it always follows the main axis.

order.title: order
order.description: Controls the order of the flex items. By default, all have order: 0. Items with a smaller value will appear first.
order.item1: An item with order: -1 will appear before one with order: 0.
order.item2: An item with order: 1 will appear after those with order: 0.
order.example: In this example, we can see how the items are ordered from lowest to highest according to their order value.
order.tip: order only changes the visual order. Keyboards and screen readers still follow the HTML order, so do not use it to reorder meaningful content.

flexShorthand.title: flex & flex-flow
flexShorthand.description: flex is the shorthand for flex-grow, flex-shrink and flex-basis, in that order. flex-flow does the same for flex-direction and flex-wrap on the container.
flexShorthand.item1: flex: initial: same as 0 1 auto. It does not grow, but it can shrink.
flexShorthand.item2: flex: auto: same as 1 1 auto. It starts from its content and shares the free space.
flexShorthand.item3: flex: 1: same as 1 1 0%. It ignores the content so items end up the same size.
flexShorthand.item4: flex: none: same as 0 0 auto. It keeps its size and neither grows nor shrinks.
flexShorthand.item5: flex-flow: row wrap: sets direction and wrapping on a single line.
flexShorthand.example: Change the value of flex on the item class and watch how it shares space with its siblings. The last value sets a base size of 12rem.
flexShorthand.tip: Use the flex shorthand instead of the three separate properties: it is shorter and avoids unexpected leftover values.

alignSelf.title: align-self
alignSelf.description: Overrides the align-items value for a single item, aligning it on the cross axis without affecting its siblings.
alignSelf.item2: flex-start: places the item at the start of the cross axis.
alignSelf.item3: center: centers the item on the cross axis.
alignSelf.item4: flex-end: places the item at the end of the cross axis.
alignSelf.item5: stretch: stretches the item along the cross axis if it has no fixed size.
alignSelf.item6: baseline: aligns the item along its text baseline.
alignSelf.example: The container aligns its children to the start, but the child with the item class can escape that rule with align-self.
alignSelf.tip: There is no justify-self in flexbox. To separate an item on the main axis use margin-left: auto, a handy pattern to push a button to the end of a bar.

alignContent.title: align-content
alignContent.description: Distributes the space between the lines of a flex container on the cross axis. It only has an effect when there are multiple lines, that is, with flex-wrap: wrap.
alignContent.item1: stretch (default): lines stretch to take up the available space.
alignContent.item2: flex-start: packs the lines at the start.
alignContent.item3: center: packs the lines in the center.
alignContent.item4: flex-end: packs the lines at the end.
alignContent.item5: space-between: the first and last lines touch the edges and the rest are spread between them.
alignContent.item6: space-around: leaves the same space around each line.
alignContent.item7: space-evenly: leaves identical spaces between lines and at the edges.
alignContent.example: This container has a fixed height and several lines. Change align-content to distribute the rows. If you remove flex-wrap in the editor, you will see it no longer has any effect.

grid.title: grid
grid.description: CSS grid is a two-dimensional layout system that allows arranging elements into rows and columns precisely, with control over spacing for both rows and columns. Unlike flexbox, which focuses on distributing items in one direction (row or column), grid enables full control of layout along both axes. Its big advantage is that you can define complex structures in a simple and adaptable way, with control over the number and size of rows and columns, spacing and alignment of elements, and reorganization of the design depending on screen size or device (responsive).

basics.title: grid & inline-grid
basics.description: The container is defined with display: grid or display: inline-grid, and its direct children become grid items that are distributed within the grid.
basics.item1: grid: The container behaves as a block that takes up all the available width.
basics.item2: inline-grid: The container behaves as an inline element, occupying only the necessary space.
basics.example: In this dynamic example, we can see how the child elements adjust depending on the value of display.

explicit.title: Explicit grid
explicit.description: This is a layout system where the grid is explicitly defined using grid-template-rows and grid-template-columns.
explicit.item1: Rows and columns are declared directly in the grid.
explicit.item2: No additional rows or columns are created unless items force them (in which case the implicit grid comes into play).
explicit.item3: Ideal for predictable layouts, where the exact number of rows and columns is known in advance.
explicit.example: In this dynamic example, since we do not handle the sizes of rows and columns that are created implicitly, these will take the height and width of the child.

implicit.title: Implicit grid
implicit.description: This is a layout system where the grid automatically expands to accommodate elements that don’t fit into the explicitly defined grid.
implicit.item1: Rows or columns not declared in the explicit grid are generated automatically.
implicit.item2: We can use grid-auto-rows or grid-auto-columns to define the size of the implicit rows/columns being created.
implicit.item3: Ideal when the number of elements is dynamic or unknown beforehand.
implicit.example: In this dynamic example, we can see how an implicit row is created, which takes the height from grid-auto-rows, and how an implicit column is created with its width defined by grid-auto-columns.

autoFlow.title: grid-auto-flow
autoFlow.description: This is the property that controls how items are automatically placed in the grid when their positions are not specified.
autoFlow.item3: dense: tries to fill gaps by reordering later items.
autoFlow.example: In this dynamic example, we can see how items are arranged according to the value of grid-auto-flow.

positioning.title: Item positioning
positioning.description: grid items can occupy specific cells or span multiple rows / columns using dedicated properties.
positioning.item1: grid-column and grid-row: define where an item starts and ends in terms of row / column.
positioning.item2: grid-area: combines start / end row and column in one property.
positioning.example: In this dynamic example, using grid-column / grid-row we tell the element with the class positioning to occupy columns 1 and 2, and rows 1 and 2. With grid-area, we tell the element with the class positioning to take rows 1 and 2 and column 3.

areas.title: grid-template-areas
areas.description: Allows defining layouts using semantic names for different grid zones.
areas.item2: Each item is assigned with grid-area: name.
areas.example: In this example, with grid-template-areas we define a layout with 3 rows and 3 columns, where each cell has a semantic name. Then, each item is positioned in the grid by assigning the corresponding name via grid-area.
areas.tip: Write a dot instead of a name to leave a cell empty. Each area must form a rectangle: it cannot be L-shaped.

functions.title: Useful functions
functions.description: Functions that simplify creating dynamic and responsive grids.
functions.item1: repeat (n, value): avoids writing the same value n times manually.
functions.item3: auto-fit: tries to fit columns to the container’s width; if there’s extra space, it collapses gaps.
functions.item4: auto-fill: similar to auto-fit, but leaves empty slots if there aren’t enough items.
functions.example: In this example, with grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(70px, 1fr)) we create as many columns as fit (auto-fit), each column will be at least 70px, and extra space is distributed proportionally (1fr). With grid-auto-rows: minmax(50px, auto), each row has a minimum height of 50px.
functions.tip: The difference between auto-fit and auto-fill only shows when there is spare space. Replace auto-fit with auto-fill in the editor using few items and compare the result.

alignment-container.title: Container alignment
alignment-container.description: Properties that control how items are aligned inside each grid cell.
alignment-container.item5: stretch: Stretches the item to fill the entire cell (default).
alignment-container.item6: start: Aligns to the start of the cell (left for horizontal, top for vertical).
alignment-container.item8: end: Aligns to the end of the cell (right for horizontal, bottom for vertical).
alignment-container.example: In this dynamic example, we can see the different alignments of cells using justify-items and align-items.

alignment-content.title: Content alignment
alignment-content.description: Properties that control how rows and columns are distributed inside the grid container.
alignment-content.item5: stretch: Stretches rows/columns to fill all available space (default).
alignment-content.item6: start: Aligns the whole grid to the start of the axis (top or left).
alignment-content.item8: end: Places all rows/columns at the end of the axis (bottom or right).
alignment-content.item9: space-around: Distributes space leaving equal margins around each row or column group (edges have half the space of the interior).
alignment-content.item10: space-between: Distributes rows/columns so the first and last are flush with the edges, and space is distributed only between them.
alignment-content.item11: space-evenly: Places perfectly equal spaces between all rows/columns and also at the edges.
alignment-content.example: In this dynamic example, we can see the different row and column alignments using justify-content and align-content.

alignment-item.title: Item alignment
alignment-item.description: Properties to align an individual item inside its own cell.
alignment-item.item1: justify-self: aligns an item horizontally in its cell.
alignment-item.item2: align-self: aligns an item vertically in its cell.
alignment-item.item5: stretch: The item stretches to fill the whole cell along that axis (default).
alignment-item.item6: start: Aligns to the start of the axis (left in horizontal, top in vertical).
alignment-item.item8: end: Aligns to the end of the axis (right in horizontal, bottom in vertical).
alignment-item.example: In this dynamic example, we can see the different alignments of an item within its own cell using justify-self and align-self.

fixed.title: Fixed grid
fixed.description: This is a layout system where the page or interface is organized using a grid with predefined column widths that do not adapt to screen size.
fixed.item2: Ideal for highly controlled layouts where content and size are predictable.
fixed.example:
In this example we have 2 rows and a maximum of 3 columns. When a fourth element is added, it automatically goes to the next row. With grid-template-rows we define the number of rows and their height, while with grid-template-columns we define the number of columns and their width.

Additionally, with row-gap we control the spacing between rows, and with column-gap the spacing between columns.

fluid.title: Fluid grid
fluid.description: This is a layout system where the page or interface is organized using a grid with flexible column widths that adapt dynamically to screen size.
fluid.item2: Ideal for layouts that require adaptability across different devices and resolutions.
fluid.example:
In this example, we use grid-template-columns to define the number of columns and their respective widths, but this time they are proportional widths relative to the container’s width. For example, the first column takes 50% of the container and the other two share the remaining width based on their fr values.

With gap, we set the spacing of rows and columns at the same time.

subgrid.title: Subgrid
subgrid.description: It is a feature of CSS grid level 2 that allows a child grid to inherit the row or column definition from the parent grid.
subgrid.item1: Used in grid-template-rows or grid-template-columns with the value subgrid.
subgrid.item2: The subgrid must span a range of columns or rows from the parent.
subgrid.example: In this example, we can see how the content class inherits the column definition from the parent container. To achieve this, we use grid-column: 1 / -1, which makes it occupy all available columns, from the first to the last.
subgrid.tip: Subgrid is ideal for aligning the titles, text and buttons of several cards, even when each one has content of a different length.

units.title: Units in grid
units.description: Apart from the basic CSS units (px, em, rem, vh, vw...), these are the most commonly used units in CSS grid:
units.item4: min-content / max-content: adjusts to the minimum or maximum content size.
units.item5: span: allows an element to span multiple rows or columns based on the specified number.
units.example: In this example, we show a series of columns with each of these units, where we can visualize the behavior of each one.
units.tip: Prefer fr over percentages when using gap: fr shares the space left after subtracting the gaps, while percentages can overflow the container.

responsive.title: Responsive with grid
responsive.description: Strategies to achieve layouts that automatically adapt to different screen sizes.
responsive.item1: Media queries: allow applying conditional CSS styles depending on the screen width.
responsive.item2: @media (max-width: ...): applies when the screen width is less than or equal to the specified value. Commonly used to adjust layouts on small screens (e.g., mobile).
responsive.item3: @media (min-width: ...): applies when the screen width is greater than or equal to the specified value. Typically used in mobile-first approaches, where the design is first defined for mobile and then extended for larger screens.
responsive.item4: Use of auto-fit and minmax() to create fluid grids that adapt without media queries, generating as many columns as can fit in the container.
responsive.item5: Use of auto-fill: similar to auto-fit, but keeps empty spaces reserved for columns that do not get filled.
responsive.item6: Combination with grid-template-areas: allows easy reorganization of the layout based on breakpoints by rearranging entire blocks.
responsive.item7: Relative units (fr, %, auto, min-content, max-content) promote flexible behavior on small screens.
responsive.item8: Modern properties like clamp() help set a minimum, ideal, and maximum width without the need for multiple media queries.
responsive.example: Move the preview width control and switch techniques with the selector. auto-fit needs no media queries, while the other two options change the structure at a breakpoint.
responsive.tip: The media queries in this example respond to the preview width because the result is displayed inside its own document.

namedLines.title: Named lines
namedLines.description: Grid lines can be named so positioning is easier to read than with numbers and does not depend on the number of columns.
namedLines.item1: Names are written in square brackets inside grid-template-columns or grid-template-rows.
namedLines.item2: A single line can have several names, separated by spaces.
namedLines.item3: If you use the -start and -end suffixes, the browser creates an implicit area with that name, usable in grid-area.
namedLines.example: The grid defines the sidebar, main and full lines. Select a grid-column value to place the element with the item class using those names.

overlap.title: Overlapping items
overlap.description: Unlike flexbox, in grid several items can occupy the same cells. This lets you create overlaps without using position: absolute.
overlap.item1: Assign items the same row and column lines, fully or partially.
overlap.item2: By default, the last item in the HTML is painted on top.
overlap.item3: With z-index you control the stacking order without needing position.
overlap.item4: Assigning grid-area: 1 / 1 to several children is a simple pattern for stacking image and text.
overlap.example: The two items share grid cells. Change the z-index value on the item class to decide which one stays in front.

boxSizing.title: box-sizing
boxSizing.description: Defines what the width and height of an element include. This property decides whether padding and border are added to the size you declared or are part of it.
boxSizing.item1: content-box (default): width and height only measure the content; padding and border are added outside.
boxSizing.item2: border-box: width and height include content, padding and border, so the final size is exactly the declared one.
boxSizing.example: Both children have the same width, padding and border. Change box-sizing on the item class and compare its final size with the reference child.
boxSizing.tip: Most projects apply box-sizing: border-box to every element with the universal selector. That way percentage widths do not overflow when you add padding.

position.title: position
position.description: Controls how an element is placed relative to the page’s normal flow. Together with top, right, bottom, left and z-index, it lets you overlap elements or pin them on screen.
position.item1: static (default): the element follows the normal flow and ignores top, right, bottom, left and z-index.
position.item2: relative: keeps its space in the flow and is offset from its original position.
position.item3: absolute: leaves the flow and is placed relative to its nearest positioned ancestor.
position.item4: fixed: leaves the flow and is placed relative to the viewport; it does not move on scroll.
position.item5: sticky: behaves as relative until it reaches the given threshold, then sticks inside its container.
position.item6: inset: shorthand to write top, right, bottom and left in a single property.
position.example: Child 2 has the item class. Change position and scroll inside the container to see how each value reacts. Notice how the other children take its space when it leaves the flow.
position.tip: An element with position: absolute needs a positioned ancestor as a reference. The usual approach is to set position: relative on the container. If sticky does not work, check whether an ancestor has an overflow other than visible.

containerQueries.title: Container queries
containerQueries.description: Container queries apply styles based on the size of the container rather than the screen. A component adapts the same way in a narrow sidebar as in a wide column.
containerQueries.item1: container-type: inline-size: makes an ancestor queryable by its width.
containerQueries.item2: container-name: assigns a name to query a specific container.
containerQueries.item3: @container (min-width: ...): applies rules when the container reaches that size.
containerQueries.item4: cqw / cqh: units relative to the container’s width and height, equivalent to vw and vh.
containerQueries.example: Reduce the preview width. The card switches from one column to two when its container exceeds 28rem, without any media query.
containerQueries.tip: An element cannot query its own size: set container-type on an ancestor and apply the changes to its descendants.

logical.title: Logical properties
logical.description: Logical properties describe layout according to the writing direction rather than left or right. Your design adapts on its own to languages such as Arabic or Japanese.
logical.item1: inline: the axis text flows along. In English it is horizontal.
logical.item2: block: the axis blocks stack along. In English it is vertical.
logical.item3: margin-inline, padding-block: replace the physical margins and paddings of each axis.
logical.item4: inline-size, block-size: equivalent to width and height in horizontal writing.
logical.item5: inset-inline-start: the logical equivalent of left in left-to-right languages.
logical.example: Change direction and writing-mode. Because the item class uses logical properties, its spacing follows the writing direction in every case.
logical.tip: Flexbox and grid are already logical: flex-start and start follow the writing direction. That is why a row flips automatically with direction: rtl.

flexVsGrid.title: Flexbox vs grid
flexVsGrid.description: Flexbox and grid do not compete: they complement each other. The useful question is not which is better, but what leads in each case, the content or the structure.

row1.label: Dimensions
row1.grid: Two: rows and columns at once

flexVsGrid.example: With the same HTML, compare both systems. In flex, items on the last line grow to fill it; in grid, they respect the columns of the previous rows.
flexVsGrid.tip: Combining them is the norm: grid for the page structure and flex for the components inside each area.

recipes.title: Layout recipes
recipes.description: Patterns that solve the most frequent everyday problems. Pick a recipe, copy it and adapt it to your project.
recipes.item1: center: centers any element on both axes with two lines of code.
recipes.item2: holy grail: header, navigation, content, sidebar and footer in a single grid.
recipes.item3: sidebar: fixed-width sidebar and content that takes the rest.
recipes.item4: sticky footer: the footer stays at the bottom even with little content.
recipes.item5: card grid: responsive cards without media queries.
recipes.example: Select a recipe. HTML and CSS update together, and you can keep editing them to adapt it.
